title: Quoting, expansion and filename boundaries
markdown:
## Why this matters

A command receives an argument vector, not the original line you typed. Losing the boundary around one filename can make an otherwise correct command act on different inputs. This lesson begins with observing arguments before applying the same reasoning to file operations.

## The simple version

Imagine labeling separate envelopes before handing them to a worker. The worker sees each envelope as one item. Quoting tells Bash which expanded text should remain in one argument. The analogy breaks because quotes also select expansion rules: double quotes still allow variable expansion, while single quotes preserve literal characters. The quote marks normally do not become part of the resulting argument.

## Core mechanics

The shell reads command syntax and performs applicable expansions before invoking a command. An unquoted parameter expansion can undergo word splitting and pathname expansion. If `name='quarterly report.txt'`, passing `$name` can produce two arguments; passing `"$name"` produces one argument containing the space.

An empty quoted expansion still supplies one empty argument. An empty unquoted expansion can disappear. Check `$#` to distinguish zero arguments from one empty argument: a formatting command can print a line even when it was supplied no data operand.

Single quotes suppress parameter expansion entirely. Double quotes expand parameters while preserving their argument boundary. Quoting should express the intended data flow; repeatedly adding quotes after a command has already split its input cannot reconstruct the lost boundaries.

## Failure modes

Asterisks in unquoted expanded data may match filenames in the working directory. That makes behavior depend on unrelated files. Literal quoting prevents this expansion, but it does not stop an external command from interpreting a leading hyphen as an option. When the command supports it, `--` marks the end of options; consult that command's documentation. These are two separate boundaries: the shell constructs arguments, then the program interprets them.

Use the observation function below before trying any copy or move operation. No file contents are needed to understand the boundary problem.

## Runnable experiment

Run this in Bash in your own terminal. It creates no files and requires no elevated permissions. Predict the output before running it.

```bash
show_args() {
  printf 'argc=%s\n' "$#"
  printf '<%s>\n' "$@"
}
name='quarterly report.txt'
show_args "$name"
# argc=1; <quarterly report.txt>
show_args $name
# argc=2; <quarterly> then <report.txt>
name=''
show_args "$name"
# argc=1; <>
show_args $name
# argc=0; printf still prints <> for its missing format operand
printf '%s\n' '$name' "$name"
# literal $name followed by one empty line
```

## Practical exercise

Extend show_args to number every argument using a for loop. Test a plain value, an empty value, a value with spaces, a literal asterisk and a leading hyphen. Use quoted expansions throughout the repaired wrapper. Record the argument count and each exact value, then explain which examples concern shell expansion and which concern option parsing.

Deliverable: A numbered argument transcript covering all five cases and a short explanation of the two parsing boundaries.

## Key takeaways

- Observe the argument vector before debugging the called program.
- Double quotes preserve boundaries while permitting variable expansion.
- Treat empty arguments, wildcard characters and leading hyphens as separate cases.

## Sources

- [Quoting](https://www.gnu.org/software/bash/manual/html_node/Quoting.html)
- [Shell Expansions](https://www.gnu.org/software/bash/manual/html_node/Shell-Expansions.html)
- [printf invocation](https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/manual/html_node/printf-invocation.html)

Use a counter and printf; do not turn the argument vector back into one string.

questions.prompt: With name="quarterly report.txt", which expression passes exactly one argument containing the full name?
questions.explanation: Double quotes preserve the expanded value as one argument. The space remains data.
questions.learning_objective: Preserve a spaced filename as one argument

questions.prompt: An empty variable is expanded as "$name". How many arguments does that expression supply?
questions.explanation: Quoted empty expansion preserves an argument; unquoted empty expansion may disappear.

questions.prompt: Why can an unquoted variable containing an asterisk behave differently after another file is created?
choices: Pathname expansion can match the new file
questions.correct_answer: Pathname expansion can match the new file
questions.explanation: The shell expands unquoted patterns using directory contents before the command receives its operands.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between single-quoting the text $name and double-quoting it.
questions.correct_answer: Single quotes pass the literal characters $name. Double quotes expand the variable while keeping the result in one argument.
questions.explanation: Quote choice governs expansion as well as argument boundaries.
questions.learning_objective: Explain the expansion rules of single and double quotes

questions.prompt: A quoted filename starts with a hyphen. Why might a command still reject it, and what should you check?
questions.correct_answer: Quoting preserves one argument, but the command may interpret that argument as an option. Check whether it supports -- before filename operands or use a documented unambiguous path form.
questions.explanation: Shell parsing and program option parsing are different stages.
